claims.text: Children receiving OSI+TS gained 0.021 QALYs using the UK adult value set compared to usual school practice.
Children receiving OSI+TS gained 0.043 QALYs using the Australia adolescent value set compared to usual school practice.
From the NHS and PSS perspective, children in the OSI+TS arm incurred an additional £244.16 compared to the USP arm.
The ICER for OSI+TS compared to USP was £11,462.47 per QALY gained based on the UK adult value set.
The ICER for OSI+TS compared to USP was £5,700.98 per QALY gained based on the Australia adolescent value set.
At a £20,000 WTP threshold per QALY gained, OSI+TS had an 88.2% probability of being cost-effective using the UK adult value set.
At a £20,000 WTP threshold per QALY gained, OSI+TS had a 99.3% probability of being cost-effective using the Australia adolescent value set.
At 12 weeks after randomization, child utilities were significantly higher in the OSI+TS arm than in the USP arm for both the UK adult and Australia adolescent value sets.
At 12 months follow-up, the difference in child utilities between the OSI+TS and USP groups was no longer statistically significant.
No statistically significant differences between trial arms were found for parents' EQ-5D-5L utilities or QALYs throughout the trial.
From a societal perspective, the total mean difference in cost between OSI+TS and USP was £234.71, which was not statistically significant.
The overall frequency of anxiety problems 12 months after randomization did not differ significantly between the OSI+TS and USP groups in the primary clinical analysis.

evidence.description: Children receiving OSI+TS gained 0.021 (95% CI 0.010-0.033; P <.001) QALYs using the United Kingdom value set.
Children receiving OSI+TS gained 0.043 (95% CI 0.021-0.064; P <.001) QALYs using the Australia value set.
From the NHS and PSS perspective, children in the OSI+TS arm incurred £244.16 (95% CI £76.26-£412.07; P =0.005) more than those in the USP arm.
In the base-case CUA analysis (NHS and PSS perspective), the estimated ICER was £11,462.47 per QALY gained based on the UK adult value set.
In the base-case CUA analysis, the estimated ICER was £5,700.98 per QALY gained based on the Australia adolescent value set.
At the £20,000 threshold, OSI+TS had an 88.2% chance of being cost-effective using the UK adult value set.
At the £20,000 threshold, OSI+TS had a 99.3% chance of being cost-effective using the Australia adolescent value set.
Adjusted mean difference at 12 weeks: UK adult value set: 0.019, 95% CI 0.006-0.032; P =.004; Australia adolescent value set: 0.048; 95% CI 0.021-0.076; P =.001.

At 12 months follow-up, the difference with the USP group narrowed and was no longer statistically significant (adjusted difference UK: 0.010, 95% CI -0.003 to 0.023, P=0.13; AUS: 0.024, 95% CI -0.003 to 0.051, P=0.08).

In contrast, no statistically significant differences in parents' EQ-5D-5L utilities and QALYs between trial arms were found throughout the trial (adjusted total parent QALY difference: 0.002, 95% CI -0.016 to 0.021, P=0.81).
From a societal perspective, total societal mean difference in cost was £234.71 (95% CI £-165.37-£634.79; P =0.24) higher for the OSI+TS group compared to the USP group.

The overall frequency of anxiety problems 12 months after randomization was low and group differences were not significant in the primary clinical analysis (89/865, 6.8% intervention vs 99/865, 11.5% usual school practice [USP]).

methodologies.name: Cost-Utility and Cost-Effectiveness Analysis alongside Cluster RCT
methodologies.description: Conducted a cost-utility analysis calculating QALYs via parent-reported CHU9D (using UK adult and Australia adolescent value sets) and secondary cost-effectiveness analysis from NHS/PSS and societal perspectives over a 12-month horizon using multilevel mixed-effects models and 10,000 bootstrap iterations on 50 multiply imputed datasets.
conditions: Children aged 4-7 years identified at risk of anxiety disorders via universal school screening
OSI+TS (7 online modules plus 8 telephone support sessions) alongside usual school provision

limitations.text: Most prior studies of digital interventions for childhood anxiety problems report on effectiveness, with limited evidence on economic outcomes.
Schools and participants were enrolled based on consent, leading to potential nonrandom sample selection where schools or families less focused on mental well-being may have opted out.
Because child anxiety problems relate to school absence, school-based screening risks excluding children not attending school.
The trial period was relatively short (one year), leaving the long-term effect of OSI+TS unknown.

CHU9D was originally developed and validated for children aged 7 to 17 years, and neither the UK adult nor the Australia adolescent value set was developed specifically for children younger than 7 years.

In two sensitivity analyses adopting a societal perspective and using the UK adult value set, the probability of cost-effectiveness fell to 59.2% at a £20,000 WTP threshold, indicating considerable decision uncertainty.

future_work.text: Future research should extrapolate trial results over the medium and longer term to address the gap regarding long-term effects of OSI+TS.
Further validation work is warranted for the CHU9D descriptive system and preference weights in preschool and early school-aged children.
Future economic evaluations should take account of evaluating the monetary value and human capital cost of children's displaced time and school absenteeism.
